claims.text: The baseline is a conventionally fabricated W–Cu composite without an engineered interfacial layer.
Conventional W–Cu composites have suboptimal thermal coupling between the tungsten and copper phases.
Conventional W–Cu composites have harmful tungsten–copper interdiffusion issues.
The proposed intervention is PVD deposition of a nanoscale WC coating on tungsten particles before sintering them into a W–Cu composite.
The intervention will produce an ultrathin WC barrier at the tungsten–copper interface after composite fabrication.
An ultrathin WC interlayer will reduce thermal resistance at the tungsten–copper interface.
An ultrathin WC interlayer will enhance phonon and electron coupling between tungsten and copper.
The WC interlayer will suppress harmful interdiffusion between tungsten and copper.
Suppressing interdiffusion will preserve the mechanical integrity of the W–Cu composite.
Suppressing interdiffusion will preserve the irradiation stability of the W–Cu composite.
The WC-interlayered W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable conventional W–Cu composite.
The WC-interlayered W–Cu composite will retain mechanical strength relative to a conventional W–Cu composite.
The WC-interlayered W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance relative to a conventional W–Cu composite.
The predicted benefit is intended to hold under high thermal flux and large temperature gradients relevant to fusion applications.
The predicted benefit is intended to hold under mechanical stresses typical of fusion-reactor joints.
The predicted benefit is intended to hold during neutron and gamma irradiation exposure relevant to fusion reactors.
A WC layer that is too thick can introduce additional interfacial thermal resistance.
A WC layer that is too thick or discontinuous can impair mechanical bonding.
